title: Characterize a cooling-water valve and diagnose stiction
physicalPurpose: Meter cooling-water flow while separating the controller request, physical valve motion, installed flow characteristic, and mechanical faults.
principalTechnique: Installed-valve characterization and position-feedback stiction diagnosis
objective: After this lesson, you can measure an installed valve curve, distinguish healthy motion, command deadband and mechanical stiction, and decide when valve maintenance is justified instead of changing controller tuning.

simplifications: The inherent rangeability-50 equal-percentage relationship is taught separately from the simulator's square-law installed flow target
Positioner lag, travel rate and a three-second hydraulic response are retained while the detailed pump curve, cavitation and fluid-property changes are omitted
Deadband and stiction are injected separately on equivalent valve benches; backlash is explained and recalled from Lesson 24 but is not relabelled as either fault
Simulator actuator status supplies independent position evidence; Structured Text does not synthesize it
Simulation-only I/O and evidence; no physical valve, pump or cooling-water system is operated

baseline.limitation: Flow and controller-request traces alone do not prove whether nonlinear response comes from the installed curve, command deadband, mechanical play, stiction, or process dynamics.

change.decision: Classify stiction only from repeated request-to-position holds and breakaway jumps with corresponding flow response; otherwise retain the run as inconclusive.

disturbances: Characterize the healthy installed curve at 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 percent
Restore 70 percent and apply identical 0.5-percentage-point opening and closing increments
Repeat the restored reversal probe three times
Restore 80 percent, enter Auto bumplessly, and request 70 m3/h on all three benches

acceptance.window: settled sample at every 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 percent manual position
70 through 72 percent opening request before first larger increment
first movement after the 70 through 75.5 percent opening probe
three independently restored 70 through 75.5 percent opening probes

abortPredicates: Any required request, position or flow is nonfinite, stale, forced or invalid
Any valve request or physical position leaves 0 through 100 percent
Any measured flow leaves 0 through 105 m3/h
Mode, authority or plant identity is inconsistent across the comparison
The valves fail to close during restoration
safety.restorationMode: Return all controllers to Manual, ramp the common simulated demand to zero, verify all three physical positions and flows reach the declared safe state, then start a fresh restored run.
safety.physicalApprovalRole: authorised process controls engineer and responsible cooling-water system owner
simulationOnlyRestrictions: No physical valve, pump or cooling-water header is operated
An injected Simulation fault demonstrates a signature but does not certify a physical diagnosis
Physical testing requires reviewed topology, positioner calibration, differential pressure, hydraulic limits, safe state, abort and restoration procedure, and explicit immediate approval

video.viewerOutcome: Characterize an installed control valve and use independent stem-position evidence to distinguish deadband from stiction before changing controller tuning.

learning.context: A regulated cooling-water flow bench uses a pneumatic globe valve and digital positioner, making controller request, physical stem position and measured flow separately observable.
learning.reason: Lesson 59 bounded model-based compensation; this lesson addresses a different mismatch in which the final control element itself does not follow a sound controller request.
theory: Inherent valve capacity and installed process flow are different relationships.
Equal-percentage travel has changing local flow gain.
Command deadband, reversal-dependent backlash and static-friction stiction have different position signatures.
A confirmed diagnosis requires repeatable request, independent position and process-response evidence.
learning.workedPrediction: The fixed-head square-law installed curve predicts 0.00, 4.00, 16.00, 36.00, 64.00 and 100.00 m3/h at 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 percent, while the reversal probe predicts a two-point deadband hold and a five-point stiction hold followed by a two-point slip jump.
practicalPreparation: Verify Simulation evidence, identities, units, quality, timing, mode, requests, physical positions, actuator states, flows, limits and safe-close restoration.
Define curve error, request-position gap, stationary time, breakaway, reversal lost motion, flow excursion and physical-position travel before results.
learning.baseline: Characterize the healthy installed curve and show why flow gain changes with position before attributing nonlinear flow to a fault.
learning.change: Change only actuator condition to command deadband or stiction and apply one equivalent opening, closing and closed-loop experiment.
learning.comparison: Keep installed curve, controller, initial position, request trajectory, timing, limits, seed and metric windows equal across all three benches.
learning.validation: Require the predicted curve points, distinct two-point deadband and five-point stiction holds, the two-point slip jump, and three independently restored reversal probes before classifying the injected fault.
learning.explanation: Integral action grows the request while static friction holds the stem; breakaway moves flow abruptly and creates a cycle that retuning can change but not repair.
learning.transfer: Use independent position feedback and repeatable probes before recommending maintenance; Lesson 61 next separates valve faults from genuine two-input, two-output process interaction.
